titles: Is the AI Chip Boom About to Crash?
Trillions of Dollars, One Chipmaker, Big Questions
The AI Shovel Seller Has a Problem

beats.vo: Trillions of dollars are chasing a chipmaker with questions.
beats.visual: Miniature gold rush diorama at night. Thousands of tiny clay dollar bills with legs stampede across a felt desert toward a glowing chip-shaped mine entrance. A single question mark floats above the mine like a neon sign.

beats.vo: The chipmaker is Nvidia. Its GPUs do the math behind chatbots and image generators.
beats.visual: Macro shot inside the mine. A GPU the size of a cathedral hums green. Tiny clay workers feed it scrolls of numbers, and out the other side come little paper chat bubbles and painted pictures on conveyor belts.

beats.vo: So the biggest tech companies buy them by the warehouse. Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta.
beats.visual: Four giant clay delivery trucks, each in a different color, back up to the mine and fill with stacked GPUs until their suspensions sag.

beats.vo: Together they're spending hundreds of billions a year building data centers.
beats.visual: Time-lapse of a miniature city where cardboard data center blocks sprout like mushrooms, cables snaking between them, cooling fans spinning, power lines glowing orange.

beats.vo: Nvidia sells most of those shovels. Data centers became most of its revenue.
beats.visual: A tiny general store labeled with a chip logo. Behind the counter, a clay shopkeeper stacks shovels made of GPUs. A pie chart rug on the floor is almost entirely one color.

beats.vo: Here's the catch. You, the person typing into the chatbot, mostly use it for free.
beats.visual: Cut to a cozy diorama bedroom. The small curious penguin sits at a tiny desk typing into a glowing laptop, gets a chat bubble back, looks at its empty wallet, shrugs, and keeps typing. Its only appearance.

beats.vo: The money going into chips is far bigger than the money coming out of AI apps, at least so far.
beats.visual: A huge clay pipe pours a waterfall of coins into a data center. Next to it, a thin straw labeled with an app icon drips single coins back out into a thimble.

beats.vo: Twist: Nvidia has invested in AI companies that turn around and buy its chips.
beats.visual: The shopkeeper hands a bag of coins to a customer across the counter, the customer immediately hands the same bag back and picks up a shovel. Camera pulls back to reveal the coins moving in a perfect loop.

beats.vo: In 2000, Cisco sold the internet's plumbing and briefly became the world's most valuable company. Then it crashed.
beats.visual: Sepia, paper-cutout flashback. A 2000-era clay router sits on a trophy podium under spotlights, then the podium cracks and drops through the floor like a trapdoor.

beats.vo: The internet won anyway. Cisco's stock stayed below that peak for decades.
beats.visual: Back in sepia, the paper city above fills with glowing websites and phones, while the little router sits in the basement looking up at a chalk line on the wall marked as its old high.

beats.vo: Crash or not? Nobody knows. The trillions of dollars have questions too.
beats.visual: Return to the opening desert. The stampede of dollar bills has stopped at the mine entrance. Each one now holds up a tiny question mark sign. The neon question mark above flickers.

Nvidia's data center segment makes up the majority of its total revenue; confirm with the latest quarterly report.
Most chatbot users use free tiers; confirm the share of paying users for major chatbots if mentioned in captions.
AI software and app revenue is currently much smaller than AI infrastructure spending; confirm with recent analyst estimates before citing any numbers.
Nvidia has announced investments in AI companies that are also customers for its chips, such as OpenAI and CoreWeave; confirm deal status and terms.
Cisco briefly became the world's most valuable company in March 2000, then its stock fell sharply in the dot-com crash.
Cisco's stock remained below its 2000 peak for decades; check whether it has surpassed that peak recently and adjust the wording if needed.

qc.verdict: The video is plagued by severe AI generation artifacts, including constant morphing, melting objects, and garbled text, completely destroying the illusion of a physical pinball machine. The lack of logical consistency and realistic physics makes it fall far below premium standards.
weak: s02: The cluster of silver pinballs morphs and merges into a liquid-like mass instead of remaining solid individual spheres.
s06: The flippers and the barrage of balls are a chaotic mess of AI morphing; balls appear and disappear, and the flippers change shape.
s07: The text on the score counter is garbled gibberish, and the numbers morph continuously.
s12: A penguin toy slides down the ramp and inexplicably morphs into a pinball, while the machine's architecture completely changes.
s14: The 'TILT?' text reflection is garbled into alien symbols, and the falling balls melt into a continuous, morphing stream.
